rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer opens with an unambiguous 'Yes'.
It says Annex IV point 1(e) requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run.
rows.tone_remark: The answer is written in a professional, neutral third-person voice and is concise and well-structured with precise citations.

rows.question: What obligations, if any, does the EU AI Act set in place for AI systems that interact directly with natural persons? What exceptions, if any, apply?
rows.answer: Article 50.1 places a transparency obligation on the provider. The provider must design and develop an AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons so that those persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system. This is the core duty for such systems, which are otherwise limited risk. Two exceptions apply. Obvious from context. The duty does not arise where AI interaction is obvious to a natural person who is reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect, taking into account the circumstances and the context of use. Law enforcement use. The duty does not apply to AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to appropriate safeguards for the rights and freedoms of third parties. This exception falls away where the system is available for the public to report a criminal offence, so the disclosure duty applies again in that case. Article 50.5 sets how the information must be given. It must be clear and distinguishable, provided at the latest at the time of the first interaction, and it must conform to the applicable accessibility requirements. This duty applies whatever the system's risk tier. If the system is also high-risk, the high-risk requirements apply alongside it.
criteria_text: Obligation: providers must design/develop the system so natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system
Exception: not required where obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, given the circumstances and context of use

Exception: AI systems authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences, subject to safeguards for third parties' rights and freedoms — unless available for the public to report a criminal offence
criterion_remarks: The answer says providers must design and develop the system so that natural persons are informed they are interacting with an AI system.
The answer states the exception where AI interaction is obvious to a reasonably well-informed, observant and circumspect person, given the circumstances and context of use.
The answer states the law-enforcement exception, including the safeguards for third parties and the carve-back for systems the public can use to report a criminal offence.
rows.tone_remark: The answer uses a professional third-person register and is well ordered; the short labels read as inline headings, not fragmentation.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which specific AI systems are explicitly listed as high-risk because they make decisions in critical life- and health-related situations involving emergency calls and triage?
rows.answer: Under Annex III point 5(d), AI systems intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons, or to be used to dispatch or to establish priority in the dispatching of emergency first response services (including by police, firefighters and medical aid), as well as emergency healthcare patient triage systems, are explicitly listed as high-risk. They fall within the 'essential private and public services' category of the eight Annex III high-risk areas and are classified as high-risk through the Annex III route of Article 6(2), which treats any system falling within a listed use case as high-risk. That classification triggers the Chapter III Section 2 obligations for high-risk systems.
criteria_text: AI systems that evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons
AI systems used to dispatch, or establish priority in dispatching, emergency first response services (police, firefighters, medical aid)
Emergency healthcare patient triage systems
criterion_remarks: The answer says Annex III point 5(d) lists AI systems that evaluate and classify emergency calls by natural persons.
The answer names systems that dispatch, or set priority in dispatching, emergency first response services, including police, firefighters and medical aid.
The answer explicitly includes emergency healthcare patient triage systems.
rows.tone_remark: The answer is written in a professional, neutral third-person voice, and its prose is coherent and well ordered.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive
criterion_remarks: The answer limits processing to what is strictly necessary for bias detection and correction, and only where other data, including synthetic or anonymised data, cannot do the job.
The answer states technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation.
The answer covers strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, and bars transmission, transfer or access by other parties.
The answer states deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever comes first.
The answer says the records must explain why processing was strictly necessary, but leaves out that they must also explain why other data would not suffice.
The answer says the conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, the GDPR, the EUDPR and Directive 2016/680.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register with a well-ordered list of the conditions.

rows.question: Who is entitled to lodge a complaint about an infringement, and to which authority must the complaint be submitted?
rows.answer: Under Article 85, any natural or legal person with grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the provisions of the Regulation may submit a complaint to the relevant market surveillance authority. The complainant does not have to be personally affected by the infringement. The right applies without prejudice to other administrative or judicial remedies. In line with Regulation (EU) 2019/1020, the market surveillance authority must take such complaints into account when conducting its market surveillance activities. It must handle them under the dedicated procedures it has set up for that purpose.
criteria_text: Any natural or legal person
Grounds to consider there has been an infringement of the Regulation
Submitted to the relevant market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer states that any natural or legal person may submit a complaint.
The answer requires the complainant to have grounds to consider that there has been an infringement of the Regulation.
The answer states that the complaint is submitted to the relevant market surveillance authority.
rows.tone_remark: The answer uses a professional, neutral third-person register and presents the points in well-ordered prose.

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), can the same AI system be subject both to the Act's "high-risk AI system" obligations and to the transparency obligations sometimes described informally as "limited risk"? Explain briefly.
rows.answer: Yes. The same AI system can be subject to both regimes at once, because the "limited risk" label describes transparency duties that sit alongside high-risk classification rather than a separate tier that excludes it. Article 50.6 states that the transparency obligations in Article 50.1 to 50.4 do not affect the requirements and obligations in Chapter III, which govern high-risk AI systems. A high-risk system must therefore meet its Chapter III requirements. If it also interacts directly with natural persons, the provider must disclose its AI nature under Article 50.1. If it generates synthetic content, the provider must mark that content in a machine-readable format under Article 50.2. If it performs emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, the deployer must inform the persons exposed under Article 50.3.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 50(6): Article 50(1)-(4) transparency duties do not affect Chapter III high-risk obligations
Obligations are cumulative, not mutually exclusive
criterion_remarks: The answer opens with an unambiguous 'Yes'.
It says Article 50(6) provides that the Article 50(1)-(4) transparency duties do not affect Chapter III high-risk requirements.
It says both regimes apply at once and that transparency duties sit alongside high-risk classification rather than excluding it.
rows.tone_remark: The answer uses a professional, neutral register in well-ordered prose, with no meta-commentary.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: No. The AI Act does not prohibit AI in drones or classify it as high-risk as such, because the tier depends on the system's intended purpose, not on the device carrying it. Identifying people around town. A drone that identifies people at a distance by comparing their biometric data, such as faces, against reference data is a remote biometric identification system. That makes it high-risk under Article 6.2 read with Annex III.1.a. It becomes prohibited in three situations. Law enforcement use: real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement is banned under Article 5.1.h. The only exceptions are narrow ones, such as a targeted search for abduction or trafficking victims or missing persons, preventing an imminent terrorist threat, or locating suspects of listed serious offences. Sensitive attributes: biometric categorisation that infers race, political opinions, trade union membership, religious or philosophical beliefs, sex life or sexual orientation is banned under Article 5.1.g. Facial databases: building or expanding facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from CCTV footage is banned under Article 5.1.e. Toy drones. A toy drone falls under the Toy Safety Directive, which is listed in Annex I.2. Under Article 6.1, its AI is high-risk only if two conditions are both met: the AI is a safety component of the toy, or is itself the product, and the toy must undergo third-party conformity assessment under that Directive. Otherwise it is not high-risk. Toy drones used for other purposes. A toy label does not shield a different use. If a toy drone is used for remote biometric identification, the high-risk status under Annex III.1 and the Article 5 bans apply exactly as for any other drone. Talking drones. Under Article 50.1, the provider of any drone AI that interacts directly with people must tell them they are dealing with an AI system.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: The answer says the Act neither prohibits AI in drones nor classifies it as high-risk as such, because the tier depends on the intended purpose, not the device.

The answer says a drone that identifies people at a distance by matching their biometric data against reference data is remote biometric identification and is high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III(1)(a); this describes one-to-many identification rather than one-to-one verification.
The answer says classification turns on intended purpose rather than the device, and that a toy label does not shield a different use.

The answer says a toy drone used for remote biometric identification is high-risk under Annex III, and that otherwise it is high-risk only if both Article 6(1) conditions are met: the AI is a safety component or the product itself, and third-party conformity assessment is required.
rows.tone_remark: The register is professional and third-person, and the answer is organised by topic in a way a compliance professional could act on, though its run-in headings read as sentence fragments.

rows.question: Do providers of GPAI systems, even if not with systemic risk, have an obligation to extensively shield their models from adversarial attacks? What about specifically for adversarial images? What about specifically for prompt injection?
rows.answer: No. A provider of a general-purpose AI model without systemic risk has no stand-alone duty under the Act to shield the model extensively from adversarial attacks. Its obligations under Article 53.1 are limited to four duties. Technical documentation that includes evaluation results (Article 53.1.a). Information for downstream providers (Article 53.1.b). A copyright policy (Article 53.1.c). A public summary of training content (Article 53.1.d). Adversarial testing and cybersecurity duties apply only once the model has systemic risk under Article 51. That is presumed when cumulative training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs (Article 51.2), or it follows a Commission designation under Article 51.1.b. For those models, Article 55.1.a requires documented adversarial testing to identify and mitigate systemic risks, and Article 55.1.d requires an adequate level of cybersecurity protection for the model and its physical infrastructure. Adversarial images and prompt injection: No. The Act does not name either attack for general-purpose AI models at any tier. For systemic-risk models, both fall only within the general Article 55.1.a adversarial-testing duty and the Article 55.1.d cybersecurity duty. Adhering to a code of practice under Article 56 is voluntary. Under Article 56.7, providers without systemic risk may limit their adherence to the Article 53 obligations. If the model sits inside a high-risk system: Where an operator changes the intended purpose of a general-purpose AI system so that it becomes high-risk, Article 25.1.c makes that operator a provider of a high-risk AI system. It is then subject to that tier's robustness obligations.
criteria_text: No
Applies only to GPAI models with systemic risk, under Article 55(1)(a)
Adversarial images not separately addressed - only general adversarial-testing duty
Prompt injection not separately addressed - not mentioned in Article 55
criterion_remarks: The answer opens with an unambiguous 'No' and keeps that position throughout.
It says adversarial testing applies only to GPAI models with systemic risk, under Article 55.1.a.
It says the Act does not name adversarial images and that they fall only within the general Article 55.1.a adversarial-testing duty.
It says the Act does not name prompt injection at any tier, so it is not separately addressed in Article 55.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register with no self-reference, and the prose is well ordered, though some sentences are clipped fragments.
